landmarks.writeup: A protected area known for its diverse wildlife and scenic landscapes, offering walking and cycling trails.

wiki.extract: Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary is Eswatini's oldest protected area, owned and managed by a non-profit trust.

landmarks.name: Mantenga Cultural Village
landmarks.writeup: A cultural site showcasing traditional Swazi life, crafts, and ceremonies.

wiki.extract: Hhohho is a region of Eswatini, located in the north western part of the country. Hhohho was named after the capital of King Mswati II, who expanded the Swazi territory to the north and west, taking in the districts of Barberton, Nelspruit, Carolina and Piet Retief. These areas were later acquired by what was the Province of Transvaal and today they form part of the Mpumalanga Province of South Africa. It has an area of 3,625.17 km2, a population of 320,651 (2017), and is divided into 14 tinkhundla. The administrative center is the national capital of Mbabane. It borders Lubombo Region on the southeast and Manzini Region in the southwest.

landmarks.name: Ngwenya Mine
landmarks.writeup: One of the oldest known mines in the world, historically significant for ancient iron ore extraction.

wiki.extract: The Ngwenya Mine is located on Bomvu Ridge, northwest of Mbabane and near the northwestern border of Eswatini (Swaziland). This mine is considered to be the world's oldest. The haematite ore deposit was used in the Middle Stone Age to extract red ochre, while in later times the deposit was mined for iron smelting and iron ore export.

cultural_events.name: Umhlanga Reed Dance
cultural_events.writeup: An annual ceremony where young women present reeds to the queen mother, celebrating chastity and unity.

wiki.extract: Umhlanga, or Reed Dance ceremony, is an annual Swazi event that takes place at the end of August or at the beginning of September. In Eswatini, tens of thousands of unmarried and childless Swazi girls and women travel from the various chiefdoms to the Ludzidzini Royal Village to participate in the eight-day event.

cultural_events.name: Incwala Ceremony
cultural_events.writeup: The 'Kingship Ceremony' marking the first fruits harvest and reaffirming the king's authority.

wiki.extract: Incwala is the main ritual of kingship in the Kingdom of Eswatini. This is a national event that takes place during the summer solstice. The main participant in incwala is the King of Eswatini; when there is no king there is no incwala. Incwala takes place over a period of time of about a month, starting with the small incwala, incwala lencane, and culminating in the big incwala, incwala lenkhulu. A number of activities - such as lusekwane, kuhlamahlama, and umdvutjulwa - mark the key events of this age old tradition. Unlike Ummemo which is convened by local chiefs, Incwala and Umhlanga are national events and are convened under the authority of the King and the Queen Mother.

food_writeup: Eswatini cuisine features staples like maize, sorghum, and meat dishes such as 'sidvudvu' (pumpkin stew) and 'emasi' (fermented milk). Traditional meals often accompany communal gatherings.
brief_history: Formerly known as Swaziland, Eswatini gained independence from Britain in 1968. It is one of Africa's last absolute monarchies, ruled by King Mswati III since 1986.
current_conflicts: Eswatini experiences occasional political unrest related to calls for democratic reforms, but no active armed conflicts.

commentary.inflation_management: Eswatini's inflation is imported from South Africa via the lilangeni's one-to-one peg to the rand and Common Monetary Area membership. It peaked at 12.7% in the 2008 commodity boom and troughed at 2.6% in 2019, tracking South African price dynamics with a small premium. The 2022 global shock lifted it only to 4.8%, and it has since eased to a projected 3.1% in 2025. The central bank shadows the South African Reserve Bank's policy, so Eswatini has no independent monetary lever; inflation management is effectively outsourced to Pretoria, which has served price stability well at the cost of policy autonomy.
commentary.debt_management: Eswatini's debt has risen steadily as SACU revenues, the fiscal mainstay, became more volatile and spending proved rigid. From 10.6% of GDP in 2009, the series low, the ratio climbed through the 2010s to 44.9% projected for 2025, the series high, with a sharp COVID-era jump from 29.8% (2019) to 38.0% (2020). The government borrows domestically and from South African markets under the Common Monetary Area. Sustainability is not yet critical, but the trajectory is one-directional, and domestic arrears to suppliers have repeatedly emerged as a shadow fiscal problem, signaling cash management stress beneath the headline ratio.

key_events.event: SACU revenue collapse triggered a fiscal crisis; South Africa's bailout offer was declined.
Global financial crisis aftershocks; debt began its steady climb from 10.6% of GDP.
COVID-19 pushed debt from 29.8% to 38.0% of GDP; SACU revenues fell.
Pro-democracy protests met with a deadly crackdown, the worst unrest in the kingdom's history; economic disruption followed.
Debt projected at a series high of 44.9% of GDP as fiscal pressures persist.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued slow growth with inflation anchored by the rand peg and debt drifting higher on rigid spending. Upside depends on SACU revenue stability and any political opening that unlocks investment; downside is that the absolute monarchy's legitimacy crisis deters the private sector indefinitely. Uncertainty is moderate on macro policy (the peg is credible) but high on politics, which is the binding constraint.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
